questions.problem:
The function $f(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(c-x)^{2}+3c, & x\ne -1, \\ -5, & x=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-1$, what are the possible values of $c?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -1}((c-x)^{2}+3c) \\  & =(c-(-1))^{2}+3c \\  & ={c}^{2}+2c+1+3c \\  & ={c}^{2}+5c+1.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x) & =f(-1) \\ {c}^{2}+5c+1 & =-5 \\ {c}^{2}+5c+6 & =0 \\ (c+2)(c+3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, $c=-2$ or $c=-3.$

The function $h(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by

$$
h(x)=\{\begin{aligned}(x-c)^{2}+1, & x\ne 2, \\ 2, & x=2.\end{aligned}
$$

If $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=2$, what are the possible values of $c?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $h(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}h(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 2}((x-c)^{2}+1) \\  & =(2-c)^{2}+1 \\  & ={c}^{2}-4c+5.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}h(x) & =h(2) \\ {c}^{2}-4c+5 & =2 \\ {c}^{2}-4c+3 & =0 \\ (c-3)(c-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, $c=3$ or $c=1.$

questions.problem:
The function $g(x)$ is given by 

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{1-x}}{ax}, & x\ne 0, \\ \frac{1}{4}, & x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

For what value of $a$ is the function continuous at $x=0?$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the limit, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{1-x}}{ax} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{1-x}}{ax}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\sqrt{x+1})^{2}-(\sqrt{1-x})^{2}}{ax(\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{ax(\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2\cancel{x}}{a\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2}{a(\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{1-x})} \\  & =\frac{2}{a(\sqrt{0+1}+\sqrt{1-0})} \\  & =\frac{1}{a}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & =g(0) \\ \frac{1}{a} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $a=4$ removes the point discontinuity.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Removing a Point Discontinuity in a Piecewise Polynomial Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $f(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189990/assets/90209edc9ee3cc9c6c17b71427dc4dda0a14558a9df7b2a71dbe017073b9086a.svg)
If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=1,$ what is the value of $k?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x),$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,1}({x}^{2}+2kx+1) \\  & ={1}^{2}+2k(1)+1 \\  & =2+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}f(x) & =f(1) \\ 2+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $k=1$ removes the point discontinuity.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Removing a Point Discontinuity in a Piecewise Exponential or Logarithmic Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $h(x)$ is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189990/assets/d113c9de6e0c7946ed9952a2a245f4ba0ebb627b74c4661a2a067216fe5099d8.svg)

Given that $h(x)$ is continuous at $x=0,$ what is the value of $c?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the definition of $h(x),$ we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}h(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0}{log}_{3}⁡(x+c) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(0+c) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡(c).\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $h(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}h(x) & =h(0) \\ {log}_{3}⁡(c) & =2 \\ c & ={3}^{2} \\ c & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $c=9$ removes the point discontinuity.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Removing a Point Discontinuity in a Piecewise Radical Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $g(x)$ is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189990/assets/c67122865cc8decbb3238cd70c1fe662bdbcf9f697bd8a8e594e4408b88a08c3.svg)
If $g(x)$ is continuous at $x=2,$ what is the value $b?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the definition of $g(x)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}g(x)={lim}_{x\to 2}(\sqrt{bx+3})=\sqrt{2b+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}g(x) & =g(2) \\ \sqrt{2b+3} & =5 \\ 2b+3 & =25 \\ 2b & =22 \\ b & =11.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)$ below.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14189990/assets/20b2fd99ae051c3447e4c3530fee053b248393147a8295d3a9451524d7534f52.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=4.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $a,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $a$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x) = f(4)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $4.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 4}(3x+a) \\  & =3(4)+a \\  & =12+a\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=4,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=13.$ So $f(4)=13,$ and we can solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & =f(4) \\ 12+a & =13 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=4,$ we need to choose $a=1.$
